claims.claim: title: "c. 58,000 prostitutes, minus 12 weeks' holiday"
claims.source: ONS 2014 (Abramsky & Drew, unsiap mirror; local extraction ons2014-flat.txt); ONS Revisions to GDP in Blue Book 2016
claims.passage: Adding these and scaling up by UK population [Assumption 5] gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country. / Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates.
claims.notes: Both numbers trace to ONS; the title compresses the holiday factor, which ONS applied to the spending estimate, without misstating it.

claims.claim: status: "still published: ONS series MNC8 runs 1985 to 2024, last released 31 October 2025"
claims.source: ONS time series MNC8 (series page and CSV generator, both fetched live this round)
claims.notes: The live CSV runs from 1985 to 2024 with release date 31-10-2025, and the series page also gives 31 October 2025.

claims.claim: teaser: "illegal drugs and prostitution in UK GDP, built on assumptions ONS called \"arbitrary\" and \"probably false\""
claims.passage: We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption. / We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it.
claims.notes: ONS uses both words about its own assumptions.

claims.claim: ledgerTitle: "The numbers: illegal activity in the UK national accounts, 2014 to 2025"
claims.passage: Date: 29 May 2014 / "Release date","31-10-2025"
claims.notes: The range runs from the earliest source (May 2014) to the latest MNC8 release (October 2025).

claims.claim: ledger: "Illegal activity added to the level of GDP (Patterson, ONS, 2014): up to £10 billion a year"
claims.source: Patterson, Civil Service Quarterly blog, 15 Oct 2014 (fetched live)
claims.passage: ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP.
claims.notes: Both the figure and the 'up to' qualifier come from Patterson, and the row credits him.

claims.claim: ledger: "Prostitutes in the UK, scaled from 2004 London estimates (ONS 2014): c. 58,000"; body: "Scaled by population, that \"gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country.\""
claims.passage: In the same year the Metropolitan Police estimated 115 prostitutes on the street at any one time in London (Home Office (2004)). Adding these and scaling up by UK population [Assumption 5] gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country.
claims.notes: The quote is verbatim, and both London inputs are from 2004.

claims.claim: ledger and body: clients per week following "a Netherlands assumption", run at 20, 25 and 30
claims.passage: Following a Netherlands assumption with some research support, quoted in Smekens and Verbruggen (2005), we calculate estimates based on 20, 25 and 30.
claims.notes: The quote and all 3 figures match.

claims.claim: ledger: "Price per visit, 2004, from Punternet (ONS 2014): £55"; body: "The price, £55 in 2004, was \"an estimate from Punternet supported by a 2004 journal article\"."
claims.passage: 2 Output Price population (Assumption 1). The method is to calculate W following an estimate from Punternet supported by a Series 2004 journal article. This is �55 in 2004.
claims.notes: 'Series' is part of the Method Area column label ('2 Output Price ... Series', matching '1 Output Volume Series' and '3 Intermediate Consumption Series') that the extraction interleaves with the text, so leaving it out is faithful; the mangled character (�) is the pound sign in '£55'. This also fixes the round 2 advisory about dropping the journal-article support.

claims.claim: body: "Footnote 12, for Punternet, is a Wikipedia URL."
claims.passage: This was estimated based on research on Punternet12 ... 12 http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punternet
claims.notes: Footnote 12 is that Wikipedia URL; the exhibit describes it and does not cite it.

claims.claim: ledger: "Illegal production, 2010: drugs / prostitution / total, % of GDP (ONS FOI reply): 0.24% / 0.35% / 0.58%"
claims.passage: Total N2 for 2010 = £9097 (million). Total GDP (Production) = £1555548 (million). N2 as % of GDP = 0.58% Drugs % of GDP = 0.24% Prostitution % of GDP = 0.35%
claims.notes: All 3 percentages are verbatim; 9097/1555548 is 0.585%.

claims.claim: ledger gap row and body: prostitution spending in 2010 was "£5.6bn (current prices)" in the FOI reply and is £4,370m in MNC8 today
claims.source: ONS FOI (fetched live); ONS MNC8 CSV (fetched live)
claims.passage: Prostitution is accounted for in COICOP 12.2 in HHFCE. The value for 2010 is £5.6bn (current prices), which is 0.4% of GDP. / "2010","4370"
claims.notes: Both figures measure COICOP 12.2 household spending at current prices, so the comparison is like for like.

claims.claim: body: "An ONS freedom of information reply of November 2015"; source entry: "released 6 November 2015"
claims.passage: Release date: 6 November 2015
claims.notes: The date matches the page.

claims.claim: body: "ONS does not attribute the difference. This site's arithmetic: £4,370m is 78% of £5.6bn, and 40 weeks is 77% of 52."
claims.source: derived from ONS FOI, MNC8, Blue Book 2016
claims.passage: The value for 2010 is £5.6bn (current prices) / "2010","4370" / Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year
claims.notes: 4370/5600 = 78.0% and 40/52 = 76.9%; every input traces, and both the body and the disclosure label the calculation as the site's own.

claims.claim: ledger: "Holiday allowed per year, from Statistics Netherlands (ONS, Blue Book 2016): 12 weeks"; body: Blue Book 2016 reduced the prostitution estimates "to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes" plus the Statistics Netherlands quote
claims.source: ONS Revisions to GDP in Blue Book 2016 (fetched live; bb2016.txt)
claims.passage: As a further refinement, allowance was made to reduce the estimates made for prostitution in household final consumption expenditure by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates.
claims.notes: Both quotes match the source exactly.

claims.claim: ledger and body: MNC8 gives £5,993m for 2019, £4,130m for 2020 and £6,431m for 2024
claims.notes: All 3 values match the live CSV.

claims.claim: ledgerNote: "MNC8 is modelled, not observed. ONS's 2014 method varied a 2004 point estimate by the 16+ male population and the CPI; the series has been adjusted since, including the 12-week holiday in Blue Book 2016."
claims.passage: The benchmark for extrapolation is set as 2004. / Volume is extrapolated using the male population aged 16+ (Census) / Price is extrapolated using CPI for Personal Services / As there is no time series, we vary the point estimates in time using the male population (Assumption 1). / As a further refinement, allowance was made to reduce the estimates made for prostitution in household final consumption expenditure by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes.
claims.notes: The 2014 method is described in the past tense and the later adjustment is acknowledged.

claims.claim: ledgerNote: "ONS publishes both 2010 figures and does not attribute the difference between them."
claims.passage: The value for 2010 is £5.6bn (current prices) / "2010","4370"
claims.notes: Both figures are live on ons.gov.uk, and none of the fetched ONS pages connects the two.

claims.claim: verdict Fraud detected: "none. Every assumption was published, many with a grade from their authors: \"weak\", \"controversial\", \"arbitrary\", \"probably false\"."
claims.passage: This is a weak assumption based on the market for prostitutes' services. / This is a controversial assumption based on reasoning from two premises. / This is an arbitrary assumption. / This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it.
claims.notes: All 4 grades are ONS's own words.

claims.claim: verdict Rules broken: "none in the 2014 method. Before it, the UK accounts left the activity out: \"This is the first time that any such estimates will have entered the UK National Accounts.\" Blue Book 2016 calls the work \"addressing a GNI ESA 1995 reservation\"."
claims.passage: Currently, the only type of illegal activity covered by the UK National Accounts is the smuggling of alcohol and tobacco ... This is the first time that any such estimates will have entered the UK National Accounts. / Illegal activities As part of addressing a GNI ESA 1995 reservation, improvements were implemented to the measurement of illegal activities in Blue Book 2014
claims.notes: Both quotes are verbatim; the row now states the pre-2014 omission and the reservation, which resolves the round 2 PARTIALLY SUPPORTED, and 'the activity' (drugs and prostitution) is accurate because ONS says smuggling was the only illegal activity already covered.

claims.claim: verdict Usefulness: "limited by ONS's own account: the estimates are \"partly based\" on assumptions, \"especially\" for prostitution. Required for comparability regardless."
claims.passage: such calculation requires a number of assumptions on which the estimates are, therefore, partly based. This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity. / Comparability between nations dictates that all countries include it in their GDP figures.
claims.notes: Both quoted words trace, and so does the comparability point.

claims.claim: verdictNote: "ONS's 2014 method says \"there is no time series\" for prostitution, and varied a 2004 point estimate by the male population and a price index."
claims.passage: As there is no time series, we vary the point estimates in time using the male population (Assumption 1). / This is varied through time using the CPI for the personal services product (CPA: 96).
claims.notes: The quote is verbatim.

claims.claim: verdictNote: "Series MNC8 now runs from 1985, 29 years before the first estimate was published."
claims.passage: "1985","1078" / This is the first time that any such estimates will have entered the UK National Accounts. / The main national accounts dataset was published on 30 September
claims.notes: 1985 to 2014 is 29 years, and the year is right whichever 2014 publication date applies.

claims.claim: verdictNote: "The chart above plots it."
claims.passage: {data.exhibit === '017' && <IllegalGdpChart />}
claims.notes: The chart is wired at line 57 (re-confirmed in round 4), it renders before the Ledger and the Verdict, and it plots MNC8.

claims.claim: body: "In 2014 the UK added illegal drugs and prostitution to its national accounts."
claims.passage: ONS will therefore be including illegal drugs and prostitution activity within the estimates of UK GDP and its components, starting with the publication of Blue Book 2014 in September 2014.
claims.notes: The change came in with Blue Book 2014.

claims.claim: body: GNI "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget"
claims.passage: Gross National Income (GNI) is an important statistic within the National Accounts. It is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: "a 2012 audit of EU methods had identified areas for improvement \"which Member States have to address by 2014.\""
claims.passage: In 2012, following a comprehensive audit of the methods used across EU countries, a number of areas for improvement were identified which Member States have to address by 2014.
claims.notes: Verbatim, and the paraphrase is fair.

claims.claim: body: ESA95, section 1.13, "states that illegal transactions to which all units involved consent are included within the production boundary"
claims.passage: The European System of National Accounts 1995 (ESA95) - see Eurostat (1996), section 1.13 - states that illegal transactions to which all units involved consent are included within the production boundary
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: ONS added: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."
claims.passage: 1 This is also the case within ESA95's successor, ESA 2010; see Eurostat (2010), section 1.79. There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10.
claims.notes: Verbatim, from footnote 1.

claims.claim: body: "ONS published the method on 29 May 2014, by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew."
claims.passage: Authors: Joshua Abramsky & Steve Drew, Office for National Statistics Date: 29 May 2014
claims.notes: The date and authors match, and 'the method' correctly describes what this article is.

claims.claim: body: it warned of "significant limitations in the availability of data", requiring assumptions on which the estimates are "partly based". "This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity."
claims.passage: The article concludes that there are significant limitations in the availability of data to calculate these estimates, and that this means that such calculation requires a number of assumptions on which the estimates are, therefore, partly based. This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity.
claims.notes: All 3 quotes are verbatim.

claims.claim: body: "In 2004 a charity, Eaves, estimated about 7,000 off-street prostitutes in London, \"by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place\"."
claims.passage: A study in 2004 by Eaves (a charity helping prostitutes) estimated that there were approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London in that year; this was done by calling numbers advertised in various media and asking how many prostitutes were in each place.
claims.notes: Verbatim; the quoted method also labels how the figure was produced.

claims.claim: body: "The Metropolitan Police estimated 115 on the street \"at any one time\"."
claims.passage: In the same year the Metropolitan Police estimated 115 prostitutes on the street at any one time in London (Home Office (2004)).
claims.notes: Matches.

claims.claim: body: Constant drug consumption per user: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it."
claims.passage: We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: Half of cannabis imported, half home-grown: "This is an arbitrary assumption."
claims.passage: We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: No government spending on drugs: "reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."
claims.passage: The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: "\"Probably false\" appears 4 times in the article."
claims.passage: This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it. / This is probably false, but it is impossible to distinguish salaried employees from self-employed individuals. / The change in inventories assumption is probably false, but there is an incentive not to hold drugs as inventories / While this is probably false, we do not have any evidence to the contrary.
claims.notes: I count exactly 4 in the extraction; 'obviously false' (twice) is a different phrase.

claims.claim: body: "Every assumption was published, many with a grade attached."
claims.passage: This is a weak assumption ... This is a controversial assumption ... This is an arbitrary assumption. ... This assumption is probably false ... This is a weak assumption as the indoor greenhouse nature of cannabis production is different to the majority of legal agriculture
claims.notes: Many assumptions in the annex carry a grade.

claims.claim: body: tracking prostitution through time by the 16+ male population is "a weak assumption", needed "because we have no time series data for the number of prostitutes"
claims.passage: We assume that the number of prostitutes has the same pattern through time as the 16+ male population. This is a weak assumption based on the market for prostitutes' services. It is necessary because we have no time series data for the number of prostitutes.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: treating every prostitute and pimp as self-employed is "a controversial assumption"
claims.passage: 3b. There is no employment in prostitution; all prostitutes and pimps are self-employed. This is a controversial assumption based on reasoning from two premises.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: "In October 2014 Peter Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote on the Civil Service Quarterly blog that \"ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!)\" put the contribution at \"up to £10 billion a year\"."
claims.passage: Posted by: Peter Patterson , Posted on: 15 October 2014 ... Peter Patterson, the Deputy Chief Economic Advisor at the ONS ... ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP.
claims.notes: Name, role, date and quotes all match; the source's spelling 'Advisor' falls outside the exhibit's quote marks.

claims.claim: body: "ESA 2010 was \"legally mandated\""
claims.passage: The latest version is legally mandated through the European System of Accounts 2010 and other statistical manuals (ESA2010).
claims.notes: In the source the phrase describes the accounting standard.

claims.claim: body: "Comparability between nations dictates that all countries include it in their GDP figures."
claims.passage: Some activities may be illegal in the UK, but that is not the case everywhere. Comparability between nations dictates that all countries include it in their GDP figures.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: chart 2014 marker label "2014: FIRST ESTIMATES IN THE ACCOUNTS (30 SEP 2014)"; caption "the first estimates entered the accounts on 30 September 2014"; aria-label "A dashed marker at 2014 shows the first estimates entering the UK accounts, on 30 September 2014"
claims.source: Patterson blog (fetched live in round 4; patterson.txt); ONS 2014 (ons2014-flat.txt)
claims.passage: Posted on: 15 October 2014 ... This year, for the first time, it will include spending on prostitution and drugs. ... The main national accounts dataset was published on 30 September, and the Blue Book itself will add further detail on 31st October 2014. / this will be introduced when revised figures for the UK National Accounts, consistent with Blue Book 2014, are published in September 2014.
claims.notes: Patterson, writing on 15 October 2014 under 'Economic impact of Blue Book 2014 changes', dates the main national accounts dataset to 30 September, and ONS 2014 says the inclusion arrives with the Blue Book 2014 figures in September 2014, so the date and the 'in the accounts' framing both trace; this resolves round 3's blocking failure.

claims.claim: chart: "EARLIER YEARS ARE BACK-CAST"; caption "Values before 2014 are back-cast"; aria-label "values before 2014 are back-cast"
claims.passage: The benchmark for extrapolation is set as 2004. / As there is no time series, we vary the point estimates in time using the male population (Assumption 1). / Both prostitution and drugs activity are assumed to start in 1960.
claims.notes: Every pre-2014 value is extrapolated from a 2004 benchmark with no observed series; round 3's advisory about 'from that method' is gone because the caption now names the later adjustment.

claims.claim: chart caption and footer: "The series is modelled, not observed" / "MODELLED, NOT OBSERVED"
claims.passage: Use point in time level to extrapolate current price and volume estimates / Volume is extrapolated using the male population aged 16+ (Census) / Price is extrapolated using CPI for Personal Services
claims.notes: ONS describes an extrapolation from a single point-in-time level, and no listed source documents an observed series.

claims.claim: chart caption: "the series has been adjusted since, including the Blue Book 2016 holiday factor"
claims.source: ONS Revisions to GDP in Blue Book 2016 (fetched live in round 4; bb2016.txt)
claims.passage: Illegal activities As part of addressing a GNI ESA 1995 reservation, improvements were implemented to the measurement of illegal activities in Blue Book 2014, as described in the article Inclusion of illegal drugs and prostitution in the UK national accounts . As a further refinement, allowance was made to reduce the estimates made for prostitution in household final consumption expenditure by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates.
claims.notes: Blue Book 2016 documents a post-2014 reduction to the prostitution HHFCE estimates, and 'including' names that as 1 example without claiming to list every revision, matching the ledgerNote's wording.
